newsitem.title: UK: Thatcher's right hand man rides to Hague's rescue.
newsitem.headline: Thatcher's right hand man rides to Hague's rescue.

text.p: Cecil Parkinson has been plucked from political retirement by a man almost 30 years his junior to be chairman of Britain's Conservative Party, a job he filled successfully for his great friend Margaret Thatcher.

Parkinson, 65, is best known for a sex scandal involving his secretary in 1983 which forced his resignation shortly after Thatcher had won a crushing election victory. The election campaign which followed the Falklands War was masterminded by Parkinson.

He stood down as a member of parliament in 1992 and now sits in the upper House of Lords. But new leader William Hague, also an acolyte of Thatcher, believes Parkinson retains the political touch needed to revive a party demolished by Tony Blair's Labour Party at the May 1 election.

Parkinson said on Friday he had never intended to return to mainstream politics. But Hague, elected leader on Thursday, had asked him to return for two years to put the party, out of power for the first time in 18 years, back on its feet.
"William Hague asked me if I would do a job for him and I have agreed to come back and work for the reorganisation of the party and the modernisation of it," Parkinson told reporters.
"If I can help to create an organisation which he can use to win the next election, then I will be very well satisfied. I am not going back into fulltime politics."
Thatcher used Parkinson as her sounding board, calling him "dynamic, full of common sense, a good accountant, an excellent presenter" in her memoirs.
Appointed Trade and Industry Secretary after the 1983 election, he was forced to resign after making his secretary, Sarah Keays, pregnant. He recently described his resignation as "very traumatic".
He returned four years later to assume the energy portfolio and his rehabilitation went a stage further in July 1989 with his promotion to Transport Secretary in a cabinet reshuffle.

Parkinson's comeback marked the first time in modern British political history that a politician forced to resign over a sex scandal made it back to the front line. But Thatcher's ousting as party leader in 1990 ended his hopes of further advancement.
A railway worker's son who became a self-made millionaire, Parkinson was an unflagging advocate of Thatcher's beliefs in private enterprise and competition.
His smooth charm helped him gain her confidence and clinch the Conservative Party chairmanship in 1981.

He was once tipped as a future prime minister. But any such ambitions were frustrated by the scandal in which Keays claimed he had reneged on promises to divorce his wife and marry her. Her child now suffers from epilepsy.
Parkinson was philosophical about his political career.

"I've always had a basic rule, which I've quoted many times in the past. It is my Parkinson's Law'. Which is: in politics people love to give you what they think you deserve and deny you what they think you want," he told Reuters in an interview in the 1980s.
"My antidote to that is to just get on with the job I've got. If you do that well there might be another job -- if you do it badly there won't."
Cecil Edward Parkinson was born in Lancaster, northern England, on September 1, 1931. He won scholarships to grammar school and Cambridge University, where he read English and law.
He was a Labour Party activist as teenager but later became convinced the Conservatives offered the right answers.
After Cambridge he married Ann Jarvis, the daughter of a wealthy builder, who helped his rise in society and business. He and his wife have three daughters.
He began as a chartered accountant, later buying a construction firm which he steered into the lucrative field of engineering.

Critics said Parkinson was not an original thinker, lacked personal strength and was as slick as his brilliantined hair. But supporters saw an affable man with managerial talent and a nose for business.
This was put to the test when he was assigned to oversee the complex sell-off of the electricity industry, the government's biggest flotation in its sweeping denationalisation drive.
His next challenge was to extend the privatisation programme into heart of trade union militancy and prepare loss-making British Coal for flotation.
